title: The Five Principles of Passive House

callouts.label: Free Heat: Sun, People, and Appliances
callouts.hint: Find the low winter sun at the far upper left with rays aimed at the house's large window.
callouts.description: The Passive House Institute says these buildings are heated mainly by the sun and by heat from people and appliances, with strategic passive cooling such as shading and night ventilation in warm months. The five principles exist to keep that free heat from leaking away.
callouts.tip: A tiny heating system works only because the envelope loses so little.

callouts.label: Continuous Super-Insulation
callouts.hint: Find the thick, unbroken rose-pink blanket wrapped along the roof and walls of the house.
callouts.description: One of the five principles: a very good thermal insulation wrapped around the whole enclosure without gaps, so heat flows through the walls, roof, and floor slowly. Chapter 11 covers continuous insulation, which also covers the studs and reduces thermal bridging.
callouts.tip: Think of a down jacket with no open zipper.

callouts.label: High-Performance Windows and Doors
callouts.hint: Find the upper-floor window with a small magnified inset showing three parallel panes of glass.
callouts.description: One of the five principles: highly energy-efficient windows. In cold climates this usually means triple glazing with a low-conductivity warm-edge spacer, gas fill, and insulated frames (Chapter 12). The window is also where winter sun gets in, so its glass must lose little heat while it admits some.
callouts.tip: A window is a hole in the wall that must also act like a wall.

callouts.label: The Interdependence Star
callouts.hint: Find the five-pointed star in the upper right corner, with each point joined to the others by thin lines.
callouts.description: This is a teaching diagram, not a rule from the standard: the five measures work as a system. Insulation without air sealing leaks, air sealing without ventilation traps stale air and moisture (Chapter 19), and weak windows or thermal bridges undo good insulation. Skip one and the others lose power.
callouts.tip: Remove any point and the star collapses.

callouts.label: Airtight Construction
callouts.hint: Find the doorway on the left of the ground floor with a round fan sealed into it and a small gauge beside it.
callouts.description: One of the five principles: a continuous, sealed air control layer, so uncontrolled air leakage is small. Leakage wastes energy and carries moisture into walls. A blower-door test, a calibrated fan in a doorway that holds the house at 50 Pa, measures it (Chapters 4 and 12).
callouts.tip: Air leaks at the details, not in the middle of the sheet.

callouts.label: Balanced Ventilation with Heat Recovery
callouts.hint: Find the box in the utility room with two crossing airstreams, one warm orange and one cool blue, and ducts leading to the rooms.
callouts.description: One of the five principles: controlled mechanical ventilation with heat recovery. A heat recovery ventilator (HRV) passes outgoing stale air and incoming fresh air through a heat exchanger, so the exhaust preheats the supply without the two streams mixing. An energy recovery ventilator (ERV) also moves moisture (Chapter 14).
callouts.tip: The streams swap heat, not air.

callouts.label: Thermal-Bridge-Free Design
callouts.hint: Find the round magnifier bubble at the base of the right-hand wall, showing a thick insulating strip between wall and foundation.
callouts.description: One of the five principles: minimize thermal bridges, which are paths of high heat flow through the enclosure, such as where a wall meets the foundation or a balcony slab runs through the wall. A thermal break there reduces a cold spot where condensation could form (Chapters 3 and 12).
callouts.tip: Insulation is only as good as its weakest junction.

callouts.label: The Result: Energy Savings
callouts.hint: Find the large rounded badge on the lower right with a downward arrow beside a small flame and a snowflake.
callouts.description: The Passive House Institute reports space heating and cooling energy savings of up to about 90% compared with typical building stock, and over 75% compared with average new builds (Passipedia). For retrofits under its EnerPHit standard it reports 75 to 90%. Savings depend on the baseline and climate.
callouts.tip: "Up to" is a ceiling, not a guarantee, and the baseline matters.
